blocks.text: Yes - you can absolutely surf at Bondi, and it's one of the easiest famous waves in the world to learn on. Bondi is a sand-bottom beach break with peaks running the length of the sand, so you'll find gentle, forgiving whitewater for beginners up the northern end and steeper, punchier waves down the south. I've surfed here in every season; the short version is North Bondi to learn, the south end for a bit more shape.
Where to surf depending on your level

Bondi is a single stretch of sand that behaves like several different waves. The northern corner is the most sheltered - it catches less swell and the sand shelves gently, so the waves are smaller and softer, which is why the surf schools run their lessons up there. Head to the middle and southern end and the beach gets steeper and punchier, where the more experienced crowd sits.

As an open beach break, Bondi throws up both lefts and rights depending on how the sandbanks are lying that week. It's fickle - a great bank one month can wash away the next - so don't expect a perfect peeling point. What you get instead is a friendly, accessible wave a short walk from a coffee.

Bondi likes a south-to-east swell with a light offshore wind from the west or north-west to hold the waves up; an onshore easterly or a big sea breeze turns it messy and crumbly. I check the swell, wind and tide before I leave the house - a rising mid-tide is usually a safe bet. Have a look at a current surf forecast and the Bureau of Meteorology tide times for the day you're planning to paddle out.

If you've never surfed, book a lesson - genuinely. A good instructor will have you standing up in the whitewater in a single session, and they'll teach you to read rips and hold your board safely. Let's Go Surfing is the long-running school based at North Bondi and includes boards and wetsuits with its lessons; check their website for current session times and prices before you go.

You don't need to own a thing to surf Bondi. Board-hire shops a short walk from the sand rent soft-tops and wetsuits by the hour. Start on a big soft foamie - it floats better, catches waves earlier and won't hurt you (or anyone else) as much as a hard board when you lose it.
A wetsuit makes it more fun year-round - a spring suit is plenty in summer, but through winter I wouldn't get in without a full steamer. You'll last far longer and enjoy it more.

blocks.title: Know the flags before you paddle out
blocks.text: The red-and-yellow flags mark the patrolled swimming area - that zone is for swimmers only, so surfers and boards must stay well clear of it. Waverley Council also restricts where hard fibreglass boards are allowed, so check the current signage and the council's beach rules before you go.

items: Learn to spot a rip - the deeper, darker, calmer-looking channels where water flows back out. Beginners should stay in the whitewater near a surf school or patrol.
Surf near other people and within patrol hours if you can; lifesavers are on the sand most days but not around the clock.
Hold on to your board and look before you take off or duck-dive, so you don't cop - or deliver - a fin to the head.
Give way to the surfer already up and riding, and don't drop in - Bondi gets crowded, and etiquette keeps it friendly.

items.q: Can beginners surf at Bondi Beach?
items.a: Yes. The northern end is sheltered, with smaller, softer waves and gently shelving sand - one of the best places in Sydney to learn. Book a lesson or hire a soft-top and stay in the whitewater to start.

items.q: Where can you surf at Bondi and where can't you?
items.a: Beginners use the north end and more confident surfers spread through the middle and south. You must stay outside the red-and-yellow swimming flags, which are for swimmers only, and Waverley Council restricts where hard fibreglass boards are allowed - check the signage on the day.

items.q: When is the surf best at Bondi?
items.a: Bondi works best on a south-to-east swell with a light offshore west or north-west wind, around a rising mid-tide. Onshore easterlies and strong sea breezes make it messy - check a live surf forecast and the tide times before you go.

items.q: Do I need my own board and wetsuit?
items.a: No. Board-hire shops a short walk from the sand rent soft-tops and wetsuits by the hour, and surf schools include gear with lessons - you can turn up empty-handed.

items.q: Is the water cold at Bondi?
items.a: It's swimmable year-round but varies with the season - mild in summer and noticeably cooler in winter. A wetsuit makes every session more comfortable, and in winter a full steamer is worth it.

blocks.text: That's the beauty of Bondi: your first wave in a soft-top or a dawn session before work, the ocean's right there for everyone. Respect the flags, check the forecast, and I'll see you out the back.
